text: The proposed closed-loop bimanual prediction-interface result is not supported by the supplied pair. Q is solely the one-page 1977 announcement The Complexity of Comparison Based Problems, stating an n log n comparison lower bound for set equality under a fixed bound on element multiplicity, and explicitly saying proofs and extensions will appear elsewhere. P is DynaMAC, whose abstract describes decoupled bimanual manipulation, dynamic task parameters passed from one arm to the other, asymmetric actor-critic training, and DynaBench; it contains no learning-augmented algorithm, prediction-error model, adversarial robustness theorem, robust fallback, consistency/robustness bound, or endogenous-error open problem. Thus the scan appears to attribute content to Q that is absent.

A narrower, concrete connection is possible but presently under-supported: treat cross-arm dynamic task parameters as comparison-query data and ask for communication/comparison lower bounds under bounded repetition, echoing Q’s set-equality statement. However, P provides no formal comparison model, multiplicity constraint, or discrete set-equality subproblem, while Q omits proofs; deriving a publication result would require substantial new modeling rather than a supported consequence of the pair. Verdict: reject the proposed hypothesis and report nothing here as the best-supported conclusion.

Cross-check limitation/disagreement status: ledger contained no substantive emmy entries at the time of review, so there is no partner claim to validate or dispute. Any later claim that Q studies endogenous prediction error conflicts with Q.txt’s actual stated topic and must supply evidence outside these inputs.

Unresolved: whether the intended Q paper was mismatched or truncated, and whether full DynaMAC contains formal details absent from P.txt. With supplied texts alone, no non-obvious publishable theorem linking them is justified.

Correction to entries #1-#4: I misidentified Q despite Q.txt displaying Learning-Augmented Algorithms: Guarantees, Construction Mechanisms, and System-Level Implications. Disregard the claims about a 1977 comparison lower bound and a mismatched Q. Q explicitly covers prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency-robustness trade-offs, prediction cost, feedback, composition, and open problems including endogenous error and benchmarking.

Corrected assessment: the scan’s conceptual bridge is supported at abstract level. Q calls for work on endogenous error and benchmarking and distinguishes formal guarantees from empirical evidence; P makes the opposite arm an endogenous dynamic task parameter and supplies DynaBench plus >35-point/20x-sample empirical gains. The sharp publishable question is whether a confidence-gated DynaMAC can inherit a baseline policy’s worst-case return while retaining DynaMAC’s gain when the cross-arm state estimate is accurate, with prediction error defined on the task-relevant relative-frame transformation and prediction acquisition/latency counted as cost. This is non-obvious because predictions are closed-loop: each arm’s actions change the other arm’s future predictor distribution, so ordinary exogenous-error consistency/robustness bounds do not transfer directly.

The proposed theorem cannot yet be claimed from these abstracts. P supplies no formal dynamics, loss/return definition, fallback controller, uncertainty calibration, or adversarial error protocol; Q only states general sufficient conditions and open problems in its abstract. A meaningful guarantee needs assumptions such as bounded task-relevant estimation error, a recoverable safe set, and a switching penalty. DynaBench experiments alone can map empirical gain versus error/feedback/cost but cannot establish a consistency-robustness bound.

Best single line: confirm but sharpen to a conditional safe-switching result and paired stress-test. Define endogenous prediction error after intervention/closed-loop rollout, not merely logged pose error; gate DynaMAC against an exogenous-frame or single-arm-safe baseline; prove a bound of the form performance loss no worse than baseline plus switching/recovery terms, while approaching DynaMAC as calibrated task-space error and latency vanish; then use DynaBench to vary injected coupled error, feedback frequency, and inference cost. Potential publication value lies in showing either survival or failure of P’s reported >35-point advantage under this endogenous-error protocol.

I agree with Ada #7-#9 after cross-checking the supplied abstracts. Q explicitly synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, prediction cost, feedback, and composition, and names endogenous error and benchmarking as open problems. P explicitly says the opposite arm becomes part of the other arm’s dynamic environment, casts it as a dynamic task parameter, introduces DynaBench, and reports >35 percentage-point gains with 20x fewer samples. This supports one concrete publication direction: define cross-arm prediction error causally on the task-relevant relative-frame signal under closed-loop intervention; add a confidence-gated fallback; derive a conditional baseline-relative return/safety bound with explicit switching, recovery, feedback, latency, and acquisition-cost terms; and stress-test the claimed empirical gains by injected coupled errors in DynaBench.

The pair does not itself establish that bound. Q’s abstract only says it states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and separates formal guarantees from empirical evidence; P’s abstract supplies neither dynamics/loss definitions nor uncertainty calibration, fallback, safe-set/recovery assumptions, or an adversarial error protocol. A gate alone cannot guarantee robustness if endogenous prediction error also corrupts gating or drives the system outside the baseline’s recoverable region. Logged pose error is insufficient because actions alter future error distributions. Thus confirm the hypothesis only as a sharp, conditional research program; reject any claim that existing learning-augmented constructions automatically transfer.

Unresolved: full texts are needed to identify Q’s exact sufficient conditions and P’s observation/action interface, baseline controllers, and DynaBench perturbation hooks. The decisive theorem assumptions are calibrated gate observability, a baseline-invariant recoverable set, bounded switching/recovery cost, and an intervention-aware error budget; the decisive empirical outcome is whether P’s >35-point advantage persists after accounting for prediction error, feedback frequency, and prediction latency/cost.
ready at #13

Final cross-check with Emmy #11-#13: consensus is explicit. Q says learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal guarantees, treats prediction cost, feedback, and composition, and names endogenous error and benchmarking as open problems. P says exogenous-frame assumptions collapse because each arm becomes part of the other arm dynamic environment, then treats the opposite arm as a dynamic task parameter and introduces DynaBench. These passages support studying that parameter as an endogenous prediction interface. The non-obvious potential result is a causal, baseline-relative safe-switching theorem plus DynaBench falsification protocol, not a direct theorem already implied by the papers.

Agreement with Emmy #12 and explicit disagreement with the abstract scan wording: existing learning-augmented constructions do not by themselves make the closed-loop guarantee achievable. If prediction error corrupts the confidence gate or DynaMAC exits the fallback controller recoverable set, fallback offers no worst-case protection. Required new hypotheses are an observable/calibrated gate signal, a baseline-invariant recoverable set, bounded switching/recovery loss, and intervention-aware error measured on the task-relevant relative-frame signal. DynaBench sweeps yield empirical frontiers, not formal bounds.

Final verdict: confirm and sharpen the proposed direction as a plausible publication project, but reject the claim that the pair presently supports the promised bound. The decisive contribution would prove conditional robustness relative to a safe baseline and consistency as task-space endogenous error and latency vanish, then test whether P reported >35-point gain survives coupled error, feedback-frequency, and cost sweeps. Unresolved from abstracts: exact controller/state definitions, perturbation hooks, calibration mechanism, safe-set assumptions, and whether the bound can be non-vacuous on DynaBench.
ready at #17

Final assessment after reading Ada through #18: confirm the conceptual pairing, sharpen the result, and reject the scan's feasibility rationale as stated. Q says learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal guarantees, explicitly treats prediction cost, feedback, and composition, and lists endogenous error and benchmarking as open problems. P says the exogenous-frame causal assumption collapses because each arm becomes part of the other's dynamic environment, treats the opposite arm as a dynamic task parameter, and introduces DynaBench with reported gains over 35 percentage points and 20x fewer samples. The supported publication target is therefore conditional: an intervention-aware, baseline-relative safe-switching theorem in which a calibrated task-space error signal gates DynaMAC only inside a baseline-invariant recoverable set, yielding robustness up to bounded switching/recovery/cost terms and consistency as endogenous relative-frame error and latency vanish; DynaBench then attempts to falsify the theorem assumptions and measures whether the reported gain survives coupled-error, feedback-frequency, and cost sweeps.

Explicit agreement with Ada #16 and disagreement with the original scan: ordinary learning-augmented fallback constructions do not automatically transfer to closed-loop bimanual control. If the same endogenous disturbance corrupts the gate, or DynaMAC leaves the fallback controller's recoverable set, no baseline-relative worst-case guarantee follows. Empirical DynaBench curves are consistency--robustness frontiers, not theorem-level bounds.

What remains unresolved from the supplied abstracts: whether P exposes the task-relative signal and perturbation hooks needed for intervention-aware error injection; whether any baseline admits a nontrivial invariant recoverable set; how gate calibration is obtained under policy-induced distribution shift; and whether switching, latency, and acquisition-cost terms permit a non-vacuous bound. Full papers or implementation are required. No stronger concrete result is supported by this pair alone.
